title: Water Utilities Hacked Across 12 States as Critical Infrastructure Visibility Fails, China Retaliates Against EU With Rare Export Blacklist
subhead: Forescout finds attacked utilities didn't know what devices they had exposed; China adds 14 EU entities including a university to its dual-use export control list in response to EU sanctions on Chinese firms tied to Russia.

sections.heading: 12 States, 100+ Water Systems Hacked — and the Utilities Couldn't See What Was Exposed
sections.body:
A coordinated cyberattack campaign targeting US water and wastewater utilities has spread to at least 12 states and over 100 municipal water systems, with hackers gaining access to core operational technology at multiple facilities. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek's office confirmed Friday that hackers accessed an Oregon water district's core operating technology, though officials declined to identify which district. In Georgia, one system experienced reduced water pressure and briefly issued a boil-water advisory. In Minnesota, at least 30 water systems were targeted and one treatment plant temporarily went offline, according to the New York Times.

The FBI and EPA issued a joint advisory on July 30 warning that between July 27 and July 30, hackers connected to internet-facing programmable logic controllers (PLCs), changed IP addresses and passwords, and caused 'loss of monitoring and control functionality.' Reported effects included loss of water pressure and flooding. The FBI noted that pressure loss could allow untreated groundwater to seep into pipes.

CBS News, citing sources, reported the attacks may be linked to Iran-backed hackers, though no attribution has been officially confirmed. The attacks targeted Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs — devices manufactured by Rockwell Automation that run on the EtherNet/IP protocol, which requires no password by default.
sections.whyItMatters: This is not a theoretical vulnerability disclosure — it's an active campaign with physical consequences. Water pressure loss and boil advisories mean the attacks crossed from digital intrusion into public health impact. The FBI's own advisory confirms operational degradation, not just probing.

sections.heading: Forescout Scan Reveals the Deeper Problem: Utilities Don't Know What's Exposed
sections.body:
Forescout's Vedere Labs published research on August 5 that reframes the crisis. Scanning for devices exposing port 44818 (EtherNet/IP) on August 3, researchers found 4,407 exposed PLCs worldwide — 65% in the United States. Of the 22 exposed devices located in cities directly targeted in the campaign, 19 were on the same mobile carrier network, suggesting a shared managed service provider configuration replicated across multiple utilities rather than independent vulnerabilities.

More than 70% of US-based exposed controllers sit behind cellular modems, meaning they're connected to the public internet via mobile carrier networks rather than enterprise wiring. A PLC behind a cellular modem with port 44818 open is an internet-accessible industrial controller — a finding that connects directly to the attack method described in the FBI advisory. Two targeted cities also exposed the web management interfaces of Sierra Wireless AirLink cellular routers, a platform Forescout has separately documented with its own vulnerabilities.

Perhaps most striking: the attacked utilities didn't know what devices they had exposed. Forescout found expired security certificates, abandoned web servers, and forgotten remote-access hostnames still reachable on the public internet. NIST's National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence launched an emergency OT visibility project in June 2026 specifically because, as the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition's Tatyana Bolton told Congress: 'Most sectors have not done an OT asset inventory. So they don't even know what they have.'

A new Water Watch Center was launched this week to help small utilities address the gap, but six years of manufacturer warnings and government advisories have reduced exposed controllers by only 47% from the 2020 peak of 7,814.
sections.whyItMatters: The infrastructure visibility failure is the story. Utilities cannot secure what they cannot see, and the cellular-modem attack surface means a single MSP misconfiguration can cascade across dozens of municipalities. This isn't a patch problem — it's an asset management crisis.

sections.heading: China Retaliates Against EU, Adds University and Defense Firms to Export Control List
sections.body:
China's commerce ministry added 14 European Union entities to its dual-use export control list on Friday, effective immediately, in direct retaliation for the EU's 21st round of sanctions against Russia that targeted 14 Chinese and Hong Kong companies. The move is unprecedented in its scope: alongside German defense giant Rheinmetall, Italian electric motor maker Lafert, and French drone developer Cavok UAS, Beijing placed Wroclaw University of Science and Technology (PWr) on the list — the first time a European university has been included.

The designation prohibits the export of dual-use items from China to the named entities, including some rare earth elements, and bars the shipment of dual-use items of Chinese origin to them. The commerce ministry called the EU's actions 'egregious.' PWr said it had not received formal notification and was unable to comment.

SCMP reports that while Beijing did not explain why it singled out the university, PWr's defense research footprint and institutional ties with China offer clear clues. The move signals Beijing's willingness to weaponize export controls beyond corporate targets and into academic and research relationships.
sections.whyItMatters: Adding a university to an export control list is a new escalatory tool for Beijing. It signals that China's retaliation toolkit extends beyond mirror-image corporate sanctions to targeting the research partnerships and talent pipelines that underpin Western defense innovation. European universities with China ties will now have to reassess exposure.

sections.heading: Cambricon Revenue Doubles as China's AI Chip Substitution Accelerates
sections.body:
Cambricon Technologies, China's leading listed AI chip designer, reported 5.996 billion yuan ($890 million) in first-half 2026 revenue, up 108% year-on-year, with net profit rising 123% to 2.311 billion yuan. Q2 revenue of 3.1 billion yuan edged the 3 billion yuan Bloomberg consensus. The results come as Beijing pushes tech firms to replace Nvidia hardware: a June Bloomberg Intelligence survey found Chinese executives expect to direct 46% of AI-accelerator budgets to locally made chips within 12 months, up from 30%.

But the filing also reveals production constraints. Inventory carrying value stood at 8.248 billion yuan, up 67% year-on-year and equal to 45% of total assets. Prepaid expenses surged 291% year-on-year. Tom's Hardware reported Cambricon aims to ship 500,000 AI accelerators in 2026 versus an estimated 116,000 in 2025 — but that target depends heavily on SMIC's 7nm-class process, where reported yields were around 20% as of April.

Cambricon's five largest clients supplied 94% of revenue in H1 2025, with Caixin identifying ByteDance as the leading buyer. A July 28 stock-incentive plan set full-year 2026 revenue targets of at least 13.5 billion yuan — more than double the H1 figure — with cumulative targets of 40.5 billion yuan through 2027 and 100 billion yuan through 2028. Morgan Stanley projects China's AI-chip self-sufficiency could reach 70% by 2030, up from 42% in 2025.
sections.whyItMatters: Cambricon's growth is real but uneven — 108% revenue growth masks concentrated customer dependence, low yields at SMIC, and inventory at 45% of assets. The 13.5 billion yuan full-year target means the company needs to nearly triple its H1 run rate, putting enormous pressure on SMIC's yield improvements.

sections.heading: SK Hynix Bets $38 Billion on Two New Fabs as Memory Demand Stays Hot
sections.body:
SK Hynix approved 54 trillion won ($38.1 billion) to build two new memory chip fabrication plants in Yongin and Cheongju, South Korea, with cleanroom openings targeted for 2028 and 2029. The investment is one of the largest single fab commitments in semiconductor history and reflects SK Hynix's conviction that AI-driven memory demand — particularly for HBM — is structural rather than cyclical.

The announcement coincides with growing concern on the supply side. Digitimes reported Friday that Nvidia is testing leaner Rubin Ultra memory configurations — lower-HBM variants of its next-generation GPU — a signal that HBM4 supply may be tighter than previously projected through 2027. The original Rubin Ultra design called for higher HBM4 stacks; testing reduced-memory versions suggests Nvidia is hedging against potential shortfalls from SK Hynix and Samsung.

China's chip exports, meanwhile, surged 117% year-on-year in July, accelerating past their H1 pace, even as the overall trade surplus widened to $112.5 billion. Much of the export surge was driven by AI-related components, though analysts note that rising prices — not just volume — are inflating figures, with import prices hitting a record 25% increase in June partly due to semiconductor shortages driving chip prices up as much as 700% on certain components.
sections.whyItMatters: SK Hynix's $38 billion bet and Nvidia's Rubin Ultra redesign tell the same story from opposite ends: memory supply is the binding constraint on AI infrastructure. If HBM4 can't scale fast enough, even the richest GPU companies will be forced to ship less capable products.

sections.heading: SpaceX Starmind Gets a Launch Date, Putin-Linked Hackers Hit Zimbra Without a Click
sections.body:
SpaceX's orbital AI compute constellation is moving from concept to timeline. Alongside its first quarterly earnings report — $7.81 billion revenue, up 92% YoY — SpaceX announced the Starmind AI1 satellite will begin prototype testing in early 2027, with mass production at a new Gigafactory-like facility called 'Gigasat' planned for later that year. Each AI1 satellite carries NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 72 Rubin GPUs, peak power output of 250 kW (up 67% from initial specs), and a 70-meter wingspan. The long-term vision is a constellation of up to 1 million satellites forming a distributed orbital supercomputer. CFO Bret Johnsen said SpaceX expects to hit $100 billion annualized revenue before year-end and has signed $6.7 billion in new cloud services contracts.

Meanwhile, Russia-linked threat group Laundry Bear is exploiting a zero-click vulnerability in unpatched Zimbra email servers, stealing 90 days of emails and authentication data without any user interaction, according to multiple security reports this week. And at Black Hat 2026, Google's Project Zero team demonstrated how hackers can turn a Pixel phone into a silent bugging device in minutes without user interaction — a reminder that zero-click attack surfaces are expanding across both enterprise and consumer platforms.
sections.whyItMatters: Orbital compute moved from PowerPoint to production timeline this week — if Starmind hits its 2027 prototype date, it creates a genuinely new category of AI infrastructure. On the threat side, the Laundry Bear campaign and Black Hat zero-click demos show that the sophistication gap between attackers and defenders continues to widen, especially in email and mobile.

sections.heading: Taiwan Posts Third-Best Export Month as Concentration Risk Grows, KOSPI Selloff Exposes Korea Discount
sections.body:
Taiwan's semiconductor exports reached $75.30 billion in July, the third-best month on record, but 78.5% of outbound shipments were concentrated in semiconductors — a ratio that underscores the island's exposure to any demand disruption. Reuters reported that total exports missed forecasts slightly, though AI demand remained solid. The concentration figure is the highest in years and highlights Taiwan's structural bet on continued AI capex.

South Korea's market told the flip side of that story. The KOSPI plunged 10.84% on July 28, driven by a selloff in Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares and forced margin deleveraging. The New Indian Express noted the crash was not fundamentally an AI story — it was a chaebol concentration and governance story. Samsung and SK Hynix dominate the KOSPI, so when chip stocks fell, the entire market fell with them. Leveraged investors who had bought shares with borrowed money were forced to sell as prices dropped, amplifying the decline. The Korea Discount — the persistent undervaluation of Korean equities relative to fundamentals — remains driven by opaque corporate governance, cross-shareholdings, and controlling-family dominance.
sections.whyItMatters: Taiwan's 78.5% semiconductor concentration in exports and Korea's 10.84% single-day crash are mirror images of the same structural dependence. When AI demand holds, semiconductor dependence looks like strength. When confidence wavers, it amplifies downside violently.

bottomLine: The week's defining tech-power story isn't a chip fab or a trade number — it's that over 100 US water systems were hacked and the utilities being attacked didn't know what devices they had connected to the internet. Forescout's finding that 86% of targeted PLCs shared a single mobile carrier network turns a diffuse threat into a systemic MSP configuration problem. On the trade front, China crossed a new line by placing a university on its export control list, and Cambricon's doubling revenue shows Beijing's chip substitution push is producing results — even as 45% inventory-to-assets and 20% SMIC yields signal the substitution is easier to mandate than to execute. SK Hynix's $38 billion fab commitment and Nvidia's leaner Rubin Ultra redesign confirm that memory supply, not compute, is the binding constraint on AI infrastructure.
